title: Finance U4·W2 — WIP and Cost-to-Cost Percent Complete
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the schedule that runs the company

The work-in-process schedule is the single most important workpaper a contractor produces. It is where cost accounting becomes revenue recognition. It drives the income statement, two balance-sheet lines, the surety’s bonding decision and the bank’s covenant test. A contractor with a wrong WIP schedule does not have small errors — it has a wrong income statement, because in construction revenue is derived, not recorded. Nobody sends an invoice that equals revenue. Revenue is computed from cost.

The cost-to-cost measure

Under the input method known as cost-to-cost, progress toward satisfying a performance obligation is measured by the ratio of costs incurred to total costs expected:

Percent complete = cost incurred to date ÷ estimated cost at completion (EAC)

Then, in strict order:

  1. Earned revenue = percent complete × total contract price (inception-to-date).
  2. Cost of revenue = cost incurred to date (inception-to-date — you do not compute it, you take it).
  3. Earned gross profit = earned revenue − cost incurred to date, which also equals percent complete × total estimated gross profit.
  4. Current-period amounts = inception-to-date amounts − prior inception-to-date amounts.

Everything is inception-to-date first and periodized second. Trying to compute a month’s revenue directly is the most common way to lose the audit trail, because the moment an estimate changes the prior periods have to be absorbed through a catch-up (Unit 4 Week 4).

The three inputs, and which one is an estimate

Only three numbers feed the calculation: contract price, cost incurred to date, and estimated cost at completion. The first two are facts you can audit — the executed contract plus approved change orders, and the job cost sub-ledger tied to the GL (Week 1). The third is an estimate, and it is the only judgment in the whole schedule. That is why the auditor spends most of the fieldwork on it and why every controller-level control in construction ultimately points at the EAC.

Contract price must include approved change orders only. Unapproved change orders and claims enter the transaction price only under the variable-consideration constraint (Unit 5 Week 1). Cost incurred must include everything: burdened self-perform labor, subcontract costs gross of retention withheld, materials delivered and installed, allocated indirect construction overhead, and equipment charges.

Worked example — Harbor Row Townhomes Phase 2

Meridian Building Group, contract HR-2:

  • Contract price including approved change orders: $4,250,000
  • Estimated cost at completion: $3,612,500 → estimated gross profit $637,500, a 15.00% margin
  • Cost incurred to date: $2,348,125
  • Billings to date (gross of retention): $2,900,000

Percent complete = $2,348,125 ÷ $3,612,500 = 65.00%.
Earned revenue = 65.00% × $4,250,000 = $2,762,500.
Earned gross profit = $2,762,500 − $2,348,125 = $414,375, which checks against 65.00% × $637,500 = $414,375.
Billings $2,900,000 exceed earned revenue $2,762,500, so the job is overbilled by $137,500 — a contract liability, covered in Week 3.

The trap: taking percent complete on revenue instead of cost

This is the error that quietly destroys a WIP schedule, and it looks completely reasonable to whoever makes it. The reasoning goes: we have billed $2,900,000 of a $4,250,000 contract, so we are 68.24% complete. Trace the consequences.

  • Billings-based percent complete = $2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%.
  • Earned revenue = 68.24% × $4,250,000 = $2,900,000 — exactly the billings. The calculation is circular. Revenue can never differ from billings, so the over/under billing column is structurally zero on every job, forever.
  • Earned gross profit = 68.24% × $637,500 = $435,000, versus the correct $414,375. Gross profit is overstated by $20,625 on this job alone.

Two things make this lethal. First, it defeats the entire purpose of the schedule: the over/under billing analysis exists to reveal the difference between what you billed and what you earned, and a revenue-based measure defines that difference out of existence. Second, it is self-concealing — the schedule still foots, the balance sheet still balances, and nothing looks wrong. The tell is structural, not arithmetic: if the overbilling and underbilling columns are all zeros, the percent complete is not being taken on cost.

The diagnostic is a single sentence. Percent complete measures inputs consumed, not invoices sent. Billing is a contractual and cash-timing event governed by the schedule of values and the owner’s payment terms; it has nothing to do with how much of the work has been performed. A contractor can bill 90% of a contract in month one if the schedule of values is front-loaded (Unit 7 Week 1), and that changes cash, not revenue.

The multi-job WIP schedule and its footing checks

Three of Meridian’s open contracts at September 30:

Meridian Building Group — contracts in progress, September 30
ContractContract priceEACCost to date% completeEarned revenueEarned GPBilled to dateOverUnder
HR-2 Harbor Row Ph 2$4,250,000$3,612,500$2,348,12565.00%$2,762,500$414,375$2,900,000$137,500—
AC-1 Ashford Commons sitework$1,800,000$1,530,000$1,147,50075.00%$1,350,000$202,500$1,282,000—$68,000
LR-4 Lakeshore Ridge clubhouse$960,000$830,000$415,00050.00%$480,000$65,000$452,500—$27,500
Totals$7,010,000$5,972,500$3,910,625$4,592,500$681,875$4,634,500$137,500$95,500

Four footing checks must pass before this schedule leaves your desk, and they take about ninety seconds:

  1. Gross profit ties across: earned revenue $4,592,500 − cost to date $3,910,625 = $681,875, which equals the earned GP column total.
  2. Over/under ties to the billing gap: billed $4,634,500 − earned $4,592,500 = $42,000, and overbillings $137,500 − underbillings $95,500 = $42,000.
  3. Cost column ties to the GL: the cost-to-date total plus costs on contracts completed during the year must equal cost of revenue on the income statement.
  4. Revenue column ties to the GL: earned revenue on open contracts plus revenue on contracts completed must equal contract revenue on the income statement.

Note that the balance sheet shows $95,500 of contract assets and $137,500 of contract liabilities, gross. They are not netted to $42,000. Netting is a presentation error and it hides an overbilled job funding an underbilled one — exactly the pattern a surety underwriter is looking for.

Percent complete above 100% and other impossibilities

Automated WIP schedules produce absurdities, and the controller’s job is to catch them before the lender does. A percent complete above 100% means cost to date exceeds the EAC — the estimate was never updated and the job has already blown through it; the EAC is stale, not the cost. Earned revenue above the contract price is the same defect one column over. Negative earned gross profit on a job with a positive estimated margin means either the percent complete moved backwards (an EAC increase, which is legitimate and produces a catch-up) or costs were miscoded onto the job. And a job at 100% complete with an open commitment balance means either the commitment should have been closed or the job is not actually finished. None of these are rounding issues; each is a specific, findable posting or estimating problem.

Periodizing: turning inception-to-date into this month

Every figure above is cumulative. The income statement needs a period, and the conversion is mechanical: this period = inception-to-date now − inception-to-date at the prior close. For HR-2, if Q1 closed at $2,762,500 of earned revenue and $2,348,125 of cost, and the prior quarter had closed at $2,145,000 and $1,823,500, then the quarter’s revenue is $617,500 and the quarter’s cost of revenue is $524,625, giving $92,875 of gross profit for the quarter.

Two rules protect this. Freeze the prior column. The prior inception-to-date figures must come from the closed prior-period schedule, not from a re-computation using today’s estimates — recomputing silently absorbs an estimate change into a prior period, which is exactly what the standard forbids. Keep every closed WIP schedule. The archive of quarterly WIP schedules is the audit trail for every catch-up entry, the source data for the fade analysis in Week 4, and the first thing an auditor or surety analyst asks for.

Input methods, output methods, and when cost-to-cost misleads

Cost-to-cost is an input method: it infers progress from resources consumed. Output methods measure progress directly — units delivered, milestones achieved, surveys of work performed, physical quantities in place. Both are acceptable; the requirement is that the measure faithfully depicts transfer of control, and that the choice is applied consistently to similar contracts.

Cost-to-cost breaks down in three recognizable situations. Front-loaded costs: a job whose early scope is expensive relative to its value — heavy sitework, deep foundations, a large mobilization — reads as more complete than it is. Inefficiency: costs incurred because of rework or a labor overrun increase the numerator without advancing the work, so a job that is going badly reports faster progress, which is precisely backwards. Materials on site but not installed: a delivered generator or curtain-wall package adds cost without transferring anything, and Unit 5 Week 1 shows the adjustment the standard requires.

The practical response is not to abandon cost-to-cost — it is auditable and cheap — but to cross-check it. On a residential job, compare percent complete to the construction milestone the superintendent reports. On a unit-price job, compare it to quantities placed. When the two measures disagree by more than a few points, one of them is wrong, and finding out which is a far better use of an afternoon than refining the schedule’s formatting.

CMA bridge

Cost-to-cost is Part 1-A External Financial Reporting — revenue recognized over time using an input method — sitting directly on Part 1-D Cost Management, because the numerator is the job cost accumulation from Week 1. The exam asks you to compute earned revenue and gross profit for a period from contract price, cost incurred and estimated cost to complete; the WIP schedule is that computation for a whole company at once, with footing checks attached.

Practice and recap

  1. Percent complete = cost to date ÷ EAC. Never billings ÷ contract.
  2. Earned revenue = % complete × contract price, inception-to-date; period revenue = ITD minus prior ITD.
  3. Earned GP = earned revenue − cost to date = % complete × estimated total GP. Prove it both ways every time.
  4. Overbillings and underbillings are presented gross: $137,500 liability and $95,500 asset, not $42,000 net.
  5. Run the four footing checks, then scan for percent complete > 100%, revenue > contract price and negative GP on profitable jobs.

Recap: the WIP schedule converts job cost into revenue through the cost-to-cost ratio; contract price and cost to date are facts while the EAC is the only estimate, so the EAC is where all the risk lives; measuring completion on billings instead of cost is circular, forces revenue to equal billings, zeroes the over/under columns and overstated Harbor Row’s gross profit by $20,625; and a schedule is not finished until earned GP, the billing gap, and both GL ties have been footed.

flashcards.back: % complete = cost incurred to date ÷ estimated cost at completion (EAC). It measures INPUTS CONSUMED, never invoices sent.

1) % complete = CTD ÷ EAC. 2) Earned revenue = % × contract price (ITD). 3) Cost of revenue = CTD (taken, not computed). 4) Earned GP = earned revenue − CTD = % × estimated total GP. Period amounts = ITD − prior ITD.

flashcards.front: Trap — % complete on revenue instead of cost
flashcards.back: Billings ÷ contract = $2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%. Earned revenue then equals billings EXACTLY — circular — so over/under billing is structurally zero on every job. GP becomes $435,000 vs the correct $414,375: overstated $20,625.

flashcards.front: The tell for a revenue-based % complete
flashcards.back: The overbilling and underbilling columns are all zeros. The schedule still foots and the balance sheet still balances — the defect is structural, not arithmetic.

flashcards.front: The only estimate in the WIP schedule
flashcards.back: The EAC. Contract price (executed contract + APPROVED change orders) and cost to date (sub-ledger tied to GL) are auditable facts. All estimation risk — and all audit attention — sits on the EAC.
Contract assets $95,500 and contract liabilities $137,500 are presented GROSS, not netted to $42,000. Netting hides an overbilled job funding an underbilled one — exactly what a surety looks for.

(1) Earned revenue − cost to date = earned GP column. (2) Billed − earned = overbillings − underbillings ($4,634,500 − $4,592,500 = $42,000 = $137,500 − $95,500). (3) Cost column ties to cost of revenue. (4) Revenue column ties to contract revenue.

questions.q: Harbor Row Ph 2: contract $4,250,000, EAC $3,612,500, cost to date $2,348,125. Earned revenue to date is:
Using the same facts, earned gross profit to date is:
questions.explain: $2,762,500 − $2,348,125 = $414,375, which equals 65.00% × the $637,500 estimated total gross profit.

questions.q: A controller computes percent complete as billings ÷ contract price ($2,900,000 ÷ $4,250,000 = 68.24%). What happens to the over/under billing column?
choices: It becomes structurally zero on every job, because earned revenue is forced to equal billings
questions.explain: 68.24% × $4,250,000 = $2,900,000 = the billings. The calculation is circular, so earned revenue can never differ from billings and the analysis is destroyed.

questions.q: Under that same billings-based error, gross profit on Harbor Row is misstated by:
A WIP schedule shows total billings $4,634,500 and total earned revenue $4,592,500. Overbillings total $137,500. Underbillings must total:
questions.explain: Billed − earned = $42,000 net, and overbillings − underbillings must equal that: $137,500 − $95,500 = $42,000.

questions.q: Those same balances should appear on the balance sheet as:
choices: A $95,500 contract asset and a $137,500 contract liability, presented gross
questions.explain: Contract assets and liabilities are presented gross. Netting conceals an overbilled job financing an underbilled one.

questions.q: A WIP schedule shows a job at 108% complete. The most likely cause is:
choices: The EAC is stale and has not been raised as costs grew
The contract price was recorded twice
questions.explain: Percent complete above 100% means cost to date exceeds the estimated cost at completion — the estimate was never updated. The cost is real; the EAC is wrong.
